title: CNAS Insights | America Must Expand AI Export Controls Amid Talks with China
gist: Despite headline Chinese advances such as Moonshot's Kimi K3 and domestic DUVi lithography tools, the US retains a compute-driven AI lead and China's chipmaking lags badly (SMIC 26% 7nm yield, ~8% chip self-sufficiency); CNAS argues Washington should expand, not trade away, export controls by closing three gaps: remote cloud access to Nvidia chips, adversarial distillation of US models, and allied servicing of chip tools in China.

insights.claim: Moonshot AI's July open-weight Kimi K3 model appeared to rival US competitors, and Chinese firms Aishengna and Yuliangsheng reportedly began mass production of deep ultraviolet immersion (DUVi) chipmaking machines, fueling claims that export controls have failed.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Headline Chinese breakthroughs are being used as negotiating leverage; discount them against capacity data.

insights.claim: The narrative that export controls have failed is incomplete: the US still leads China in AI and much of China's recent progress has depended on American technology.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Supports thesis that US frontier labs and Nvidia retain a durable lead while controls hold.
insights.quote: The United States still leads China in AI, and much of China’s recent progress has depended on American technology.

insights.so_what: The US frontier lead is measured in months, not years, so it is fragile.

insights.claim: According to Goldman Sachs, China can only domestically produce around 8 percent of the advanced AI chips it needs.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: China remains structurally dependent on foreign or smuggled/remote compute.

insights.claim: SMIC's 7-nanometer yield is estimated at just 26 percent versus TSMC's 90 percent, and Huawei's leading Ascend 950 is roughly half as powerful as Nvidia's four-year-old H100.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Supports Nvidia/TSMC competitive moat versus Chinese substitutes in the near term.
insights.locator: China’s chipmaking efforts suffer from similar

insights.claim: Aishengna plans to produce five DUVi systems this year and Yuliangsheng is targeting 12, about one-eighth of the 130 DUVi machines ASML expects to ship in 2026, and SMIC still makes its most advanced chips on ASML tools.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Chinese lithography substitution is years from threatening ASML's volumes.
insights.locator: China’s chipmaking efforts suffer from similar

insights.claim: Chinese companies have remotely accessed an estimated one million H100-equivalents of compute, including export-controlled Nvidia Blackwell chips, through cloud providers in Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, about one-twentieth of the world's compute.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Southeast Asian cloud/data-center demand is partly Chinese remote access and is exposed to a regulatory crackdown.

insights.claim: Remote access to export-controlled chips is a gray area because the US Department of Commerce does not interpret its authority to cover it.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A legislative fix such as the Remote Access Security Act would hit offshore GPU rental to Chinese clients.

insights.claim: Anthropic reported the largest distillation attack it has ever observed, carried out by Alibaba, using 3,500 accounts to extract 151 million exchanges from Claude.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Distillation erodes the returns on frontier-lab training capex and is a policy flashpoint for Alibaba.
insights.quote: The campaign used 3,500 accounts to extract 151 million exchanges from Claude.

insights.claim: US AI labs cannot stop adversarial distillation individually and are constrained from cooperating by antitrust uncertainty; the FBI, NSA and CISA have urged information sharing but no concrete action has been taken.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Watch for antitrust safe-harbor guidance enabling lab coordination.

insights.claim: Continued, legal servicing of chipmaking equipment in China by ASML and Tokyo Electron lets Chinese chipmakers extend machine life to up to 30 years and transfers tacit know-how that aids reverse engineering.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: China servicing revenue at ASML and Tokyo Electron is at risk if the US pressures allies.

insights.claim: The purpose of export controls is not to prevent Chinese chip indigenization forever but to widen and lengthen the US lead, and China has pursued self-sufficiency regardless since at least 2014's National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund.
insights.speaker: CNAS
entities: National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund
insights.so_what: Undercuts the argument that controls merely accelerate Chinese substitution.
insights.quote: The purpose of U.S. export controls was never to prevent indigenization forever; it is to widen and lengthen the U.S. lead by slowing Chinese development of chips and AI.

insights.claim: Many export-control gaps could be closed by passing the bipartisan MATCH Act and Remote Access Security Act, alongside pressing allies to halt servicing in China.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Passage would tighten rules for chip-tool makers and offshore cloud providers.
insights.locator: As the next U.S.-China leader summit

insights.claim: The window to use export-control leverage is narrow, because controls only bite while Chinese firms depend on American and allied systems; once China routes around them, the leverage disappears.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Time-limited US leverage raises urgency and odds of tighter controls near-term.
insights.quote: Once China routes around U.S. and allied chipmaking technologies, that leverage will disappear.
insights.locator: The window to act is narrow

insights.claim: Ahead of the September 24 Trump-Xi summit, Washington should expand rather than weaken technology protections, since unclosed gaps let Chinese firms erode US AI companies' global market share and deepen dependence on weaponizable Chinese systems.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Any summit concession on chips would be a negative signal for US AI competitiveness.
